| # | Item | Type | Place/Date | Repository |

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

A passenger manifest could name Thomas's wife, children, and age, and potentially the Irish county or townland of origin. A naturalization declaration of intent or oath of citizenship sometimes listed accompanying family members. Irish emigrants during the Famine period commonly embarked from Liverpool or Cork for Philadelphia, Baltimore, or New York. Naturalization records for Schuylkill County are also held in Pennsylvania court records on FamilySearch. Variant spellings Flinn and Flin should be tried.

Required for a parentage question (BCG Standard 14). The 1850 census (S1) placed the Flynn household at dwelling 84, family 91; the 1860 census (S2) placed them at dwelling 112. Both records are already in the tree but only as sources for the Flynn household itself. This item targets the neighboring households enumerated adjacent to those dwellings. Irish immigrant communities in the Schuylkill County anthracite coal region frequently clustered by townland or county of origin. Neighbors sharing the Flynn surname or Irish-sounding surnames may be kin or may have emigrated from the same Irish parish; their records — baptisms, marriages, wills, letters — may identify Thomas Flynn's wife or place of origin. This is a FAN (relatives, neighbors, associates) search, not a new name search for Patrick or Thomas.

Thomas Flynn (~62) and Patrick Flynn (~35) were both in Schuylkill County from at least 1850; Thomas's 1880 household would name his wife and her birthplace, which would identify Patrick's mother. Patrick's own 1880 entry would confirm his parents' birthplaces (expected Ireland). This is the highest-yield census year for identifying the mother. Variant spellings Flynn and Flinn should both be searched.

The 1860 U.S. Federal Census (collection 1473181, name-searchable) is cited as source S2 on the parent-child relationship between Thomas and Patrick in the project tree, but has not been formally searched and extracted as a research source for q_001 — the research log for this question is empty. Thomas Flynn's 1860 household would list all co-residents: Patrick (~15) likely still lived at home, and the household should show a wife (Patrick's mother) and any siblings. Searching with variant spellings Flynn and Flinn.

A dedicated search for the marriage record of Thomas Flynn and Patrick's mother — required for every parentage plan. The marriage record would (a) confirm Thomas and his wife as a couple, (b) supply the mother's maiden name which census records omit, and (c) by its date relative to Patrick's birth (~1845) corroborate Thomas as the father named only by indirect census and derivative death-certificate evidence. Two name-searchable Pennsylvania collections cover this window: Pennsylvania Civil Marriages, 1677-1950 (collection 1571957) and Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages, 1700-1900 (collection 1502909). Date range reflects Thomas born ~1818 marrying at ~20-37 and Patrick born ~1845 as a likely early child. Note: the marriage record alone does not prove Patrick is their child — a record placing him in their household is also required.

Patrick was born in Ireland (~1845), but if Thomas and his wife had children born in Schuylkill County after emigrating, their Catholic baptism entries would name both parents — Thomas Flynn and his wife with her maiden name. This is the required FAN item for a parentage question: potential siblings of Patrick are associates whose baptism records bear directly on who Patrick's mother was. The Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records collection (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, name-searchable, personCount 982,415) covers Catholic and other denominations. The locality guide notes Catholic parishes in the anthracite region were under the Diocese of Philadelphia. Variant spellings Flynn and Flinn should be searched.

Volume 007936751 (Schuylkill County Church Records, 1842-1895) is browse-only (personCount 0) and covers parish registers not yet indexed in the Schuylkill County Church Records collection. The locality guide warns that some church films in the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups. If the indexed search in pli_004 yields no siblings' baptisms or family entries, browse this volume image-by-image for Flynn and Flinn baptism and marriage records naming Thomas and his wife.

The locality guide (loc_001) confirms probate records are held at the Schuylkill County Register of Wills from 1811. A will or letters of administration for Thomas Flynn naming Patrick as a son would be strong direct parentage evidence. S4 (Schuylkill County Probate Records) appears in the project tree as a gedcomx source but no assertions have been extracted from it for q_001 — a formal search and image browse is needed. Thomas's lifespan (born ~1818) sets the window's lower bound; he could plausibly have died from ~1855 onward.

Thomas Flynn (born ~1818, Ireland) was in Schuylkill County by 1850 and likely sought naturalization there. Pre-1906 declarations of intent and final papers sometimes name the petitioner's wife and children, and may identify his county and parish of origin in Ireland — which would enable subsequent Irish parish research to find Patrick's baptism and the family's origin. Volume 007936750 (Schuylkill Naturalization Records, 1849-1915) is browse-only (personCount 0) and requires image-by-image review. Thomas's arrival before 1850 and plausible naturalization within the first decade of residence set the target range.

By 1870 Thomas Flynn (~52) may still head a Schuylkill County household that includes his wife; Patrick (~25) may have established his own nearby household. The 1870 census records birthplace for each person (not parents' birthplaces) — Thomas's wife, if present, would be named and her birthplace recorded. Collection 1438024 is name-searchable. This fills the evidence gap between the 1860 and 1880 censuses and tracks whether Thomas and his wife remain together.

The 1900 U.S. Federal Census (collection 1325221, name-searchable) records each person's birth month and year, and — critically — a separate column for the birthplace of each person's mother and father. Patrick Flynn (~55 in 1900) would list his parents' birthplaces (expected Ireland). The 1900 census also fills the evidence gap in the decade before Patrick's death (1908), confirms his continued presence in Schuylkill County, and may show adult children or nearby siblings who share knowledge of the family's origin. Variant spellings Flynn and Flinn should be searched.

If Thomas Flynn survived past 1906 — when Pennsylvania civil death registration began — his death certificate would name his parents and possibly his wife and children. Thomas (born ~1818) would be ~88 in 1906, which is elderly but not impossible. Collection 2255317 (Pennsylvania Death Certificates, 1906-1968) is name-searchable and a quick check. Thomas's plausible lifespan sets the window; he most likely died before 1906, but if a certificate exists it would provide strong parentage evidence for Patrick. Plan written successfully. Here is the full return.

Mode: **Create** — first plan for q_001, "Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?"

**Tree survey findings that bear on the question:**
- Patrick Flynn (I1): birth ~1845, Ireland (1850 census gives age 5, birthplace Ireland — the question text says "PA" but the tree source records Ireland); death 1908-03-12, Schuylkill County, PA (death cert S3, cert no. 4521, already in tree)
- Thomas Flynn (I2): birth ~1818, Ireland; no death date or place in tree; no wife or spouse recorded
- Relationship R1 (Thomas → Patrick, parent-child): cited to 1850 census (indirect inference from household position and shared surname), 1860 census (S2, cited in tree but never formally searched and extracted for q_001 — research log for q_001 is empty), and Patrick's death certificate (derivative source for parentage)
- Patrick's 1908 Pennsylvania death certificate (S3) is already obtained but its parentage fields have not been extracted as assertions for q_001 — these fields should be extracted before new searches are initiated
- S4 (Schuylkill County Probate Records) is listed as a tree source but carries no assertions for q_001; a formal search is needed
- Patrick's mother is entirely unknown in the project

**Plan pl_002 — 10 items in execution order:**

- pli_004: census, Schuylkill County PA, 1880, FamilySearch — the 1880 census (collection 1417683, name-searchable) is the first U.S. census to state each person's relationship to the head of household and record each person's father's and mother's birthplace; Thomas's 1880 household names his wife; Patrick's own entry gives his parents' birthplaces
- pli_005: census, Schuylkill County PA, 1860, FamilySearch — 1860 census (collection 1473181, name-searchable) cited in tree as S2 but not formally extracted for q_001; Thomas's household at that date should show wife (Patrick's mother) and any siblings with Patrick (~15) likely still at home
- pli_006: vital_record (marriage), Pennsylvania, 1838-1855, FamilySearch — dedicated parents' marriage search (collections 1571957 and 1502909, both name-searchable); supplies the mother's maiden name and corroborates Thomas as father, though does not by itself prove Patrick is their child
- pli_007: church, Schuylkill County PA, 1842-1870, FamilySearch — indexed Schuylkill County Church Records (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, name-searchable); targets baptisms of siblings of Patrick born in Pennsylvania after the family emigrated — siblings' baptisms name both parents and are the required FAN item for this parentage question
- pli_008: church, Schuylkill County PA, 1842-1895, FamilySearch — browse-only volume 007936751 (personCount 0); image browse for parish registers not yet indexed; fallback for pli_007
- pli_009: probate, Schuylkill County PA, 1855-1920, FamilySearch — Thomas Flynn's will or letters of administration (collections 1999196 and volume 007936749, both browse-only (personCount 0)); naming Patrick as son would be direct parentage evidence; Thomas's lifespan bounds the window
- pli_010: immigration, Schuylkill County PA, 1849-1875, FamilySearch — Thomas Flynn's naturalization declaration, volume 007936750, browse-only (personCount 0); may name wife and children, and may identify Irish county/parish of origin to enable subsequent Irish research
- pli_011: census, Schuylkill County PA, 1870, FamilySearch — 1870 census (collection 1438024, name-searchable); fills gap between 1860 and 1880, names Thomas's wife if still living together
- pli_012: census, Schuylkill County PA, 1900, FamilySearch — 1900 census (collection 1325221, name-searchable); records separate columns for father's and mother's birthplaces; Patrick (~55) would give his parents' birthplaces and the household may show nearby kin
- pli_013: vital_record (PA death certificate), Pennsylvania, 1906-1920, FamilySearch — quick name check (collection 2255317, name-searchable) for Thomas Flynn's death certificate if he survived past 1906; his lifespan bounds the window

**Fallback relationship:** pli_008 is the fallback for pli_007 — if the indexed Schuylkill church records yield no Flynn siblings' baptisms, browse volume 007936751 image-by-image.

**Baptism note:** Patrick's baptism exists in Ireland but the parish is unknown (the unknown being sought). His 1908 Pennsylvania death certificate (S3) is already in the project tree and its parentage fields cover the same ground a death/burial item would — extraction of S3's parentage data is the priority before new searches run.

**Scope:** 10 searches (8 FamilySearch name searches or image browses + 2 browse-only volumes as fallback/primary).

Hand-back: **search-records** (FamilySearch) for all 10 items. The delegation did not authorize execution — would you like to proceed with executing this plan?

---

This plan targets the question of who Patrick Flynn's parents were. Patrick was born around 1845 in Ireland and died in 1908 in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania. The tree already connects him to Thomas Flynn through three census and death-certificate citations, but those are all indirect or derivative — no record yet names Thomas as his father in a primary, firsthand way, and his mother is entirely unknown. Before any new search is run, the parentage fields on Patrick's 1908 death certificate are already in hand and should be read first, since a Pennsylvania certificate from that period names the informant-stated father and mother. The plan then looks in ten places, beginning with the 1880 census because it is the first U.S. census to record what each person's relationship to the head of household is and where each person's father and mother were born — Thomas's wife would appear there by name. The 1860 census is second because it is already referenced in the tree but never formally extracted, and Patrick at fifteen was almost certainly still living with his parents. A dedicated search for Thomas's marriage record follows, which is required on every parentage plan: the marriage names the mother and her maiden name that census records leave out. Church records in Schuylkill County are next, searching for baptisms of any siblings of Patrick born after the family arrived — each such baptism names both parents, which makes it the single most direct route to the mother's name. A browse of an unindexed church-records volume serves as a fallback. The plan then searches Thomas's probate file (a will naming Patrick as son is the strongest possible parentage evidence), his naturalization papers (which sometimes name wife and children and can identify the Irish parish of origin), the 1870 and 1900 censuses, and finally a quick check for Thomas's own death certificate if he survived past 1906 when Pennsylvania began civil registration.

The next step is to begin executing these searches against FamilySearch, starting with the 1880 and 1860 censuses while the death certificate's parentage fields are extracted in parallel.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

entry.rationale: Thomas Flynn (born ~1818, Ireland) is the probable father of Patrick — established by 1850/1860 census co-residence (indirect) and the 1908 death certificate (direct but secondary informant). A will or letters of administration naming Patrick as a son or heir would be direct evidence of parentage, the highest-yield remaining item. Date range is sized to Thomas's likely lifespan as the record's creator: born ~1818, plausible death 1848-1885 (ages 30-67), not to Patrick's research window. S4 is already defined in the project tree as Schuylkill County Probate Records (Register of Wills).

FamilySearch 'Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records' (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) is name-searchable (personCount 982,415) and covers 1708-1985. Patrick's birth is placed ~1845; the 1850/1860 censuses say Ireland while the 1908 death certificate says Pennsylvania — both possibilities warrant a name search. A baptism or confirmation entry in Schuylkill County would place Patrick's birth in Pennsylvania and may name Thomas and his wife (Patrick's mother), providing direct and indirect parentage evidence. loc_001 notes RC parishes in Schuylkill County sat under the Diocese of Philadelphia; sacramental registers are at the parish or diocese. Even if Patrick was born in Ireland, an early post-immigration confirmation record may appear in the Schuylkill County collection.

A dedicated search for the marriage of Thomas Flynn to Patrick's mother is required for this parentage question. Patrick's mother is entirely unknown — she does not appear in the project tree and no existing source names her. The couple's marriage record would supply her maiden name (if this was her first marriage) and confirm them as a unit, corroborating parentage otherwise resting on indirect census evidence and a secondary-informant death certificate. FamilySearch SYNTH-PA-CHURCH (name-searchable) is the primary route for a Schuylkill County marriage. Date range reflects a possible post-immigration marriage 1845-1855; Thomas likely emigrated ~1845-1848 given Patrick's birth in Ireland per census. If no PA record is found, Irish church records are the next jurisdiction. Note: the marriage date relative to Patrick's ~1845 birth corroborates fatherhood but does not by itself establish that Patrick is their child — a record placing the child with the parents remains necessary for a proved conclusion.

If the name searches in items 2 and 3 return nothing, browse image group 007936751 (187 images, church records 1842-1895, browse-only (personCount 0)). loc_001 notes that some anthracite-region church films are browse-only image groups. This volume includes German-language records (languages: en, de); a name-indexed search may miss entries in German-language registers that served Irish immigrant communities alongside German-speaking parishioners. Image-by-image browsing could surface baptism or marriage entries not captured by the index.

FAN item required for this parentage question — Thomas Flynn's own court records that speak to Patrick's parentage. Image group 007936750 (298 images, Schuylkill County Naturalization Records 1849-1915, browse-only (personCount 0)) may name Thomas's county of origin in Ireland, his family members, and the witnesses who stood for him. Witnesses in Irish immigrant naturalization petitions were frequently neighbors and kin — each is a FAN lead. Thomas's stated Irish origin is the key missing fact that would open the Irish church searches needed to find Patrick's mother and confirm the family's home parish. Date range reflects the typical naturalization window for an Irish anthracite-region immigrant arriving ~1845-1848.

Proof summary ps_001 explicitly names the 1870 census as a remaining gap. In 1870 Thomas Flynn would be ~52 and may still head a Schuylkill County household. The 1870 census listed all household members by name, age, and birthplace; finding Thomas with a wife would name Patrick's mother for the first time in any extant source. Patrick (~age 25) may still appear in Thomas's household or may have his own. The 1870 census did not state relationships (that column was added in 1880), so household co-residence with shared surname remains indirect evidence, but naming the wife is the primary goal here.

Proof summary ps_001 explicitly names the 1880 census as a remaining gap. The 1880 census was the first to state the relationship of each household member to the head — if Patrick appears in any household in 1880, his stated relationship is direct evidence. Patrick (~age 35) would likely head his own household by 1880. The 1880 census also recorded each person's parents' birthplaces; those fields would confirm an Irish origin for both of Patrick's parents and further corroborate the parentage conclusion.

Proof summary ps_001 explicitly names the 1900 census as a remaining gap. Patrick (~age 55) would appear as head of his own household in Schuylkill County in 1900. The 1900 census recorded immigration year and years in the US; if Patrick's parents were Irish-born immigrants, those fields would corroborate an emigration date consistent with the family's appearance in the 1850 census and may help narrow the Irish place of origin.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

items.question: Did Michael Sheahan move to Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania around 1882 for anthracite coal-mining work, as family tradition holds?
items.rationale: log_001 places Michael as a farmer in a different county in 1870; log_002 places him in Schuylkill County by 1882 with occupation 'miner'. The occupation and location both changed between these two points, consistent with a work-driven relocation to the anthracite coal region, but nothing yet directly documents the move itself or its cause -- no land purchase, employment record, or correspondence has been found. entry.rationale: The tree records Michael Sheahan as a farmer in Pennsylvania in 1870 but gives no county. The United States Census, 1870 (collection 1438024) is name-searchable and would establish his exact county of residence, household members, and confirm his occupation as farmer -- anchoring the 'before' side of the migration question. Variant spellings Sheehan, Shehan, and Sheeahan should be tried alongside Sheahan.

The 1880 census falls between the tree's 1870 Pennsylvania entry and its 1882 Schuylkill County entry, making it the decisive record for narrowing when the move occurred. If Michael appears in Schuylkill County in 1880 as a miner, the relocation predates 1882 and aligns with the anthracite coal boom of the mid-1870s; if he appears elsewhere, the move happened in the narrow 1880-1882 window. The 1880 census also records each person's birthplace and parents' birthplaces, useful for confirming a likely Irish-immigrant origin. The United States Census, 1880 (collection 1417683) is name-searchable.

The loc_001 entry notes that Irish coal miners in the anthracite region were predominantly Catholic and that sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese level. The Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records collection (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) is name-searchable and covers 1708-1985. A sacramental record for Michael after his arrival -- a marriage, a child's baptism, or a burial entry -- would document when he was in Schuylkill County and confirm his presence in a mining-community parish, directly corroborating the work-driven relocation. Variant spellings Sheehan and Shehan should be searched.

Volume 007936751 holds Schuylkill County church records for 1842-1895 and is browse-only (personCount 0). If the name-searchable SYNTH-PA-CHURCH collection returns nothing, this image browse of the county's parish registers should be consulted directly, working through the registers for Catholic mining-town parishes such as those in Pottsville and Minersville.

The surname Sheahan is characteristically Irish, suggesting Michael may have emigrated from Ireland. Volume 007936750 holds Schuylkill County naturalization records for 1849-1915 and is browse-only (personCount 0). If Michael naturalized in Schuylkill County, his declaration of intent or certificate would state his birth county in Ireland, his US arrival date, and his Schuylkill residence -- directly corroborating both when he arrived in the county and potentially why he chose this destination over others.

The 1900 census recorded how many years a person had been in the United States -- a key field for a potentially Irish-born subject. If Michael is found in Schuylkill County in 1900 as a miner, this confirms long-term coal-region residence after the circa-1882 arrival and the immigration year recorded would help date his US arrival. A subject still mining in 1900 after arriving circa 1882 would support the hypothesis that coal work drove and sustained the relocation. The United States Census, 1900 (collection 1325221) is name-searchable.

The Miners' Journal (Pottsville, Schuylkill County) was the principal newspaper of the anthracite coal region and regularly published mine accident reports, worker lists, labor union notices, and mine company hiring announcements. A mention of Michael Sheahan in this period would directly document his presence as a working miner and potentially name his employer -- the closest available proxy for a coal company payroll record. This is an external-site search; the researcher should search Newspapers.com or Ancestry's historical newspaper holdings for the Miners' Journal and variant spellings of the surname.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

If Thomas and wife married in Ireland before emigrating, no Pennsylvania record will exist; if they married locally, this collection is the primary source. Search Thomas Flynn as groom; also Flinn and Flin variants.

Thomas Flynn (~52 in 1870) may still appear as head of household, potentially with his wife (Patrick's mother). Patrick (~25 in 1870) may still reside in the household or nearby. The United States Census, 1870 collection (FamilySearch) is name-searchable. If Thomas had died by 1870, his widow may appear as head, which would supply the mother's name. An external_collections entry (ancestry:7163) shows Ancestry also holds the 1870 U.S. Federal Census (paid) as a fallback. Search variants: Flynn, Flinn, Flin.

The 1880 U.S. Census is the first federal enumeration to record each person's relationship to the head of household and each person's parents' birthplaces (Father's Birthplace, Mother's Birthplace columns). Patrick (~35 in 1880) would appear; his stated parents' birthplaces corroborate or challenge the Ireland origin of Thomas and his unknown wife. The United States Census, 1880 collection (FamilySearch) is name-searchable. If Thomas is still alive (~62), his household could identify Patrick's mother. The 1890 federal census was largely destroyed and is not planned. Search variants: Flynn, Flinn, Flin.

The 1900 U.S. Census records each person's parents' birthplaces and adds months and year of birth. Patrick (~55 in 1900) would appear. The United States Census, 1900 collection (FamilySearch) is name-searchable. Parents' birthplaces corroborate Ireland origin. Patrick may also be enumerated with a spouse or widowed mother still living. Search variants: Flynn, Flinn, Flin.

Patrick Flynn's own church records: marriage, confirmation, and possibly a baptism if he was baptized in Pennsylvania. No spouse is recorded in the project tree, so his marriage status is unknown. Mode: **create** — first plan for q_001 ("Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?")

- I1 (Patrick Flynn): Birth ~1845, Ireland (derived from 1850 census, S1). Death 1908-03-12, Schuylkill County, PA (S3, death cert no. 4521). Parent in tree: Thomas Flynn.
- I2 (Thomas Flynn): Birth ~1818, Ireland (no source attached to him). One recorded child: Patrick.
- Relationship R1: sourced from S1 (1850 census, dwelling 84, quality 2), S2 (1860 census, dwelling 112, quality 2), and S3 (death cert no. 4521, quality 2) — all indirect (co-enumeration or derivative) with no parentage assertions yet extracted from S2 or S3 for q_001.
- S4 (Schuylkill County Probate Records, Register of Wills): in the tree sources but attached to no person or relationship; no assertions drawn from it.
- Proof summary ps_001 (tier "possible"): states only the 1850 census has been formally searched for q_001; the mother is entirely unknown.

**pl_002 — 10 items, sequence order:**

- pli_004 — vital_record, Schuylkill County PA, 1908, FamilySearch — S3 (death cert no. 4521) is in the tree but its parentage content has not been extracted for q_001; a 1908 Pennsylvania death certificate records parents' names and birthplaces; highest-yield item for direct evidence
- pli_005 — census, Schuylkill County PA, 1860, FamilySearch — S2 (dwelling 112) is in the tree on R1 at quality 2 but not extracted for q_001; may identify Patrick's mother if she was in the household; name-searchable (United States Census, 1860 collection)
- pli_006 — probate, Schuylkill County PA, 1860-1890, FamilySearch — Thomas Flynn's will or estate administration; S4 is in tree sources, unattached; browse-only (personCount 0), image group 007936749 (1851-1930); a will naming heirs is direct parentage evidence; date range sized to Thomas's plausible lifespan (~1818 birth)
- pli_007 — church, Schuylkill County PA, 1840-1875, FamilySearch — dedicated item for Thomas Flynn and his wife's marriage to each other; yields the mother's maiden name; name-searchable (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, personCount 982,415)
- pli_008 — census, Schuylkill County PA, 1870, FamilySearch — Thomas (~52) or Patrick (~25); may show Patrick's mother if she survived; name-searchable; Ancestry 1870 census (ancestry:7163) is available as a paid fallback
- pli_009 — census, Schuylkill County PA, 1880, FamilySearch — first census with relationship-to-head field and parents' birthplaces columns; Patrick (~35); name-searchable (United States Census, 1880)
- pli_010 — census, Schuylkill County PA, 1900, FamilySearch — records parents' birthplaces; Patrick (~55); name-searchable (United States Census, 1900)
- pli_011 — church, Schuylkill County PA, 1860-1910, FamilySearch — Patrick's own church records (marriage, confirmation); no spouse in tree; a marriage naming parents is direct evidence; name-searchable (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH); supplemental browse of image group 007936753 (county marriage records, browse-only, 1870-1910)
- pli_012 — military, United States, 1861-1900, FamilySearch — Patrick was 16-20 during the Civil War; name-searchable (Civil War Soldiers Index); pension file at NARA often contains parentage data; date range covers pension filing through 1900
- pli_013 — court, Schuylkill County PA, 1845-1880, FamilySearch — FAN item: Thomas Flynn's naturalization papers (image group 007936750, 1849-1915, browse-only); naturalization filings sometimes name a wife; loc_001 confirms Schuylkill County naturalization films are browse-only

Subject's death/burial item when baptism may not exist: pli_004 (Patrick's 1908 death certificate). Patrick was born in Ireland ~1845; his Irish parish baptism register is inaccessible without knowing the parish. The death certificate and marriage records (pli_011) are the primary routes to that origin.

Total scope: 10 searches (8 FamilySearch name searches or image browses, 1 NARA military follow-up).

Hand-back: search-records for pli_004 through pli_013 (all are FamilySearch collections or FamilySearch-held image groups, except pli_012's NARA follow-up which goes to search-external-sites). The delegation did not authorize execution, so this is offered rather than started.

---

The plan addresses the core question of who Patrick Flynn's parents were. It opens with his 1908 death certificate, already in the project file but not yet read for what it says about his parents — Pennsylvania certificates from that era routinely recorded both parents' names and their birthplaces, so this is the single most likely record to answer the question directly. From there the plan works through the 1860 census household (which may show his mother), his candidate father Thomas Flynn's probate file and naturalization papers (which could name the widow or confirm the family unit), the church records for Thomas and his wife's own marriage (the source of the mother's maiden name), three later censuses where Patrick himself would list his parents' birthplaces, Patrick's own church marriage record, and a check for Civil War service (whose pension file often names next of kin). All variant spellings — Flynn, Flinn, Flin — are to be tried throughout.

When you are ready, searching can begin with the death certificate and 1860 census on FamilySearch.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1840-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

entry.rationale: The FamilySearch tree for Thomas Kerrigan (ZZKR-TH2) already links source SD-KER-BAP, citing his baptism on 14 March 1842 at St. Patrick's Church, Pottsville, and naming father Patrick Kerrigan and mother Mary Gallagher; sponsors were John Gallagher and Bridget Kerrigan. This is direct primary evidence of parentage and is the highest-priority item. Search the Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records collection (name-searchable) to extract and verify the original entry; try variant spellings Carrigan and Kerigan if the standard form misses. The project tree has no parents yet documented for I2.

The FamilySearch tree also links SD-KER-1850, citing the 1850 US federal census household of Patrick Kerrigan (35, laborer, Ireland), Mary (32, Ireland), and Thomas (8, born Pennsylvania) in Pottsville, Schuylkill County. Household co-residence in 1850 corroborates the baptism entry by placing Thomas with the same two parents eight years later. Extract and verify the original image. The record is also available on Ancestry (1850 United States Federal Census — Schuylkill County, per curated external links).

A dedicated search for the marriage record of Patrick Kerrigan and Mary Gallagher, required for any parentage question. The couple married before Thomas's christening in March 1842; if they were already in Pottsville, the register at St. Patrick's (within the Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records collection, name-searchable) should hold the entry. The marriage: (a) confirms them as a unit; (b) supplies primary evidence of Mary's surname Gallagher, which pli_001 records only as a secondary annotation; and (c) by its date relative to Thomas's March 1842 birth, corroborates that Patrick was Mary's husband at the time of conception. Note: the marriage alone does not place Thomas with them — that link is established by pli_001 and pli_002. If the Pottsville search yields nothing, the couple may have married in County Mayo, Ireland before emigrating, which would require a separate Ireland search.

Thomas would be approximately 18 in 1860 and may still be living in the Kerrigan household. The United States Census, 1860 (collection 1473181, name-searchable) allows a direct name search. Finding Thomas listed with Patrick and Mary in 1860 extends the household co-residence evidence a decade past 1850 and adds a second census corroboration of pli_001. Search also for Patrick Kerrigan directly to confirm his continued presence in Pottsville.

Patrick Kerrigan died in 1880; the June 1880 census enumeration may capture him shortly before his death. Thomas, approximately 38 by then, would likely be in his own household nearby. The United States Census, 1880 (collection 1417683, name-searchable) would confirm Patrick's age (approximately 65), birthplace (Ireland), and presence in Pottsville, corroborating the earlier census and baptism entries. Thomas appearing in a nearby household would further tie him to Patrick as a son living in the same community.

Patrick Kerrigan died in 1880 in Pottsville; the date range is set to his plausible death and probate window, not Thomas's research years, because the creator of a probate record is the decedent's estate. Search the Schuylkill County Probate Records image group (volume 007936749, 1851-1930, browse-only (personCount 0)) for Patrick Kerrigan entries. A will naming Thomas as a son or an administration bond listing him as heir would be direct parentage evidence independent of the baptism record. Because this is a browse-only volume, images must be scanned page by page for Kerrigan entries. The broader Pennsylvania Probate Records collection (1683-1994) is also browse-only (personCount 0) and may duplicate coverage.

Thomas Kerrigan died in 1898 in Pottsville. Pennsylvania statewide civil death registration did not begin until 1906 (locality entry loc_001), so his death is recorded only in church burial registers or cemetery records. Search the Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records collection (name-searchable) for a burial entry. A church burial record may state his age, birthplace, or parents' names as secondary information, providing a second independent source linking him to Patrick Kerrigan and Mary Gallagher.

FAN item (required for a parentage question). John Gallagher and Bridget Kerrigan served as sponsors at Thomas's 1842 baptism — a role conventionally taken by relatives. John Gallagher's relationship to Mary Gallagher (possibly her brother or other kin) would corroborate Mary's surname and family background; Bridget Kerrigan's relationship to Patrick Kerrigan (possibly his sister) would support his place in the family. Search the Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records collection (name-searchable) and the 1850 US census for John Gallagher in Schuylkill County. Finding their family connection to either Patrick or Mary establishes independent FAN evidence for both candidate parents.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.

Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
